Text:
**Linear (mixed‑integer) model for the quarterly production‑planning problem**  

The model below contains all the data that appear in the description, the decision variables that are needed to keep track of production, inventory, and late‑delivery (back‑order) quantities, the objective function that minimises the total penalty (compensation for late delivery + storage cost), and the set of linear constraints that enforce the logical and physical restrictions of the problem.  
All indices, parameters and variables are defined first, then the complete formulation is presented.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(P=\{1,2,3\}\) | Set of products (1 = product I, 2 = product II, 3 = product III) |
| \(T=\{1,2,3,4\}\) | Set of quarters (1 = Q1, … , 4 = Q4) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Value (unit) |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| \(d_{pt}\) | Contracted demand (units) for product *p* in quarter *t* (Table 1‑10) | see table below |
| \(h_{p}\) | Production time (hours) required for one unit of product *p* | \(h_{1}=2,\;h_{2}=4,\;h_{3}=3\) |
| \(H\) | Production‑time capacity per quarter (hours) | 15 000 |
| \(c^{\text{late}}_{p}\) | Compensation cost for each unit of product *p* delivered late (per quarter) | \(c^{\text{late}}_{1}=c^{\text{late}}_{2}=20,\;c^{\text{late}}_{3}=10\) |
| \(c^{\text{store}}_{p}\) | Storage cost for each unit of product *p* kept in inventory for one quarter | \(c^{\text{store}}_{p}=5\) (same for all three products) |
| \(I^{\text{end}}_{p}\) | Required inventory at the **end** of quarter 4 | 150 (for every *p*) |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ value large enough to deactivate production of product I in quarter 2 (any number ≥ the maximum possible production, e.g. 10 000) | – |
| \(\delta_{pt}\) | Indicator for the equipment‑replacement restriction (1 if production of product p is allowed in quarter t, 0 otherwise) | \(\delta_{12}=0\) (product I in Q2), all other \(\delta_{pt}=1\) |

The demand data \(d_{pt}\) are taken directly from the table:

|          | Q1 | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 |
|----------|----|----|----|----|
| **Product I**   | 1500 | 1000 | 2000 | 1200 |
| **Product II**  | 1500 | 1500 | 1200 | 1500 |
| **Product III** | 1000 | 2000 | 1500 | 2500 |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \(x_{pt}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Number of units of product *p* **produced** in quarter *t* |
| \(y_{pt}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Number of units of product *p* **delivered** (i.e., shipped) in quarter *t* |
| \(I_{pt}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Inventory** of product *p* at the **end** of quarter *t* (after production, delivery and possible back‑orders) |
| \(b_{pt}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Back‑order (late‑delivery) quantity** of product *p* carried from the end of quarter *t* to the next quarter (i.e., units that were demanded in quarter *t* but not yet delivered) |
| \(z_{1t}\) | Binary | “Equipment‑restriction’’ indicator: \(z_{1t}=1\) forces \(x_{1t}=0\) when \(\delta_{1t}=0\). In practice we only need it for quarter 2 ( \(z_{12}=0\) ), all other quarters may have \(z_{1t}=1\). |

(If the modeler prefers to avoid binary variables, the restriction can be expressed directly as \(x_{12}=0\); the binary variable is shown only to illustrate a typical “big‑M’’ formulation.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Model formulation  

#### 4.1 Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; Z \;=\;
\sum_{p\in P}\sum_{t\in T}
\Bigl(
c^{\text{late}}_{p}\; b_{pt}
\;+\;
c^{\text{store}}_{p}\; I_{pt}
\Bigr)
}
\]

*Explanation* –  
* \(b_{pt}\) is the amount of product *p* that is **late** at the end of quarter *t*; each such unit incurs the compensation cost \(c^{\text{late}}_{p}\).  
* \(I_{pt}\) is the amount stored at the end of quarter *t*; each stored unit incurs the storage cost \(c^{\text{store}}_{p}\).  
The objective therefore minimises the total expected penalty over the planning horizon.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.2 Production‑time capacity  

\[
\sum_{p\in P} h_{p}\,x_{pt}\;\le\; H \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{C1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.3 Equipment‑replacement restriction (product I cannot be made in Q2)  

A simple linear way:

\[
x_{12}=0
\tag{C2}
\]

(If a big‑M binary formulation is preferred: \(x_{1t}\le M\,z_{1t}\) and \(z_{12}=0\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.4 Inventory‑balance (flow) equations  

For each product *p* and each quarter *t* the amount that is **available** at the beginning of the quarter is the inventory left over from the previous quarter plus any back‑order that has been carried forward (the back‑order is exactly the unmet demand of the previous quarter). The amount shipped in the quarter must satisfy the contracted demand **plus** any back‑order that existed at the start of the quarter, less the new back‑order that will be carried to the next period.

A compact formulation is:

\[
\underbrace{I_{p,t-1}}_{\text{inventory from previous quarter}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{b_{p,t-1}}_{\text{late demand from previous quarter}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{x_{pt}}_{\text{production this quarter}}
\;-\;
\underbrace{y_{pt}}_{\text{delivery this quarter}}
\;=\;
\underbrace{I_{pt}}_{\text{ending inventory}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{b_{pt}}_{\text{new back‑order}}
\qquad\forall p\in P,\; t\in T
\tag{C3}
\]

with the convention \(I_{p0}=0\) and \(b_{p0}=0\) (no initial stock and no initial shortage).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.5 Demand‑fulfilment (definition of back‑order)  

The amount shipped cannot exceed the amount that is *required* (contracted demand) plus the backlog that existed at the start of the quarter:

\[
y_{pt}\;=\; d_{pt}\;+\;b_{p,t-1}\;-\;b_{pt}
\qquad\forall p\in P,\; t\in T
\tag{C4}
\]

Because \(b_{pt}\ge 0\), this equation automatically forces \(y_{pt}\le d_{pt}+b_{p,t-1}\).  
If the modeler prefers to keep \(y_{pt}\) as a free variable, (C4) can be replaced by two inequalities:

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{pt} &\le d_{pt}+b_{p,t-1} \\
y_{pt} &\ge d_{pt}+b_{p,t-1}-b_{pt}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall p,t
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.6 End‑of‑horizon inventory requirement  

\[
I_{p4}\;=\; I^{\text{end}}_{p}\qquad\forall p\in P
\tag{C5}
\]

i.e. 150 units of each product must be on hand after quarter 4.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.7 Non‑negativity  

\[
x_{pt}\ge 0,\; y_{pt}\ge 0,\; I_{pt}\ge 0,\; b_{pt}\ge 0
\qquad\forall p\in P,\; t\in T
\tag{C6}
\]

If the binary variable \(z_{1t}\) is used, then

\[
z_{1t}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. Summary of the complete MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\; & \sum_{p\in P}\sum_{t\in T}
\bigl( 20\,b_{pt}\; (p=1,2) \;+\; 10\,b_{pt}\; (p=3)
      \;+\; 5\,I_{pt}\bigr)   \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
& \sum_{p\in P} h_{p}\,x_{pt} \le 15000 &&\forall t\in T \tag{C1}\\
& x_{12}=0 && \text{(product I cannot be made in Q2)} \tag{C2}\\
& I_{p,t-1}+b_{p,t-1}+x_{pt}=I_{pt}+b_{pt} &&\forall p\in P,\;t\in T \tag{C3}\\
& y_{pt}=d_{pt}+b_{p,t-1}-b_{pt} &&\forall p\in P,\;t\in T \tag{C4}\\
& I_{p4}=150 &&\forall p\in P \tag{C5}\\
& x_{pt},y_{pt},I_{pt},b_{pt}\ge 0 &&\forall p,t \tag{C6}\\
& I_{p0}=0,\; b_{p0}=0 &&\forall p\in P
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6. Remarks & modelling assumptions  

* **Back‑order interpretation** – A unit that is not delivered in the quarter in which it is demanded is counted as a *back‑order* (late delivery). The same unit can stay in back‑order for several quarters; each quarter it remains late incurs the compensation cost again (the objective term \(c^{\text{late}}_{p} b_{pt}\) captures this cumulative effect).  
* **Storage cost** – Inventory is charged a flat \$5 per unit per quarter, irrespective of product type (the same coefficient is used for all *p*).  
* **Production‑time capacity** – The only capacity limitation is the total number of machine‑hours available each quarter (15 000 h). No separate limit on the number of units of a specific product is imposed, except the equipment‑replacement restriction for product I in Q2.  
* **Big‑M value** – If the binary variable formulation is used, any \(M\ge\) the maximum feasible production of product I in a quarter (e.g. 10 000) is sufficient.  
* **Linearisation** – All relationships are linear; the model is a pure linear programme (LP) when the binary restriction (C2) is written as a simple equality \(x_{12}=0\). If the user wishes to keep the restriction as a “conditional’’ statement (produce only if allowed), the binary variable \(z_{1t}\) and a big‑M constraint can be added, turning the model into a mixed‑integer linear programme (MILP).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7. How to solve  

The model can be entered into any standard LP / MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, GLPK, etc.). Because the only integer requirement is the single equality \(x_{12}=0\), the problem is essentially an LP; the optimal solution will give the quarterly production quantities \(x_{pt}\), the resulting inventories \(I_{pt}\), and the back‑order levels \(b_{pt}\) that minimise the sum of compensation and storage costs while satisfying all contractual and capacity constraints.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Thus the complete linear model is provided above.**

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model**

The model determines the quarterly production quantities of three products (I, II, III) while allowing inventory carry‑over and shortage (back‑order).  The objective is to minimise the total monetary cost consisting of shortage penalties and inventory‑holding charges, subject to production‑time capacity, a forbidden‑production rule, and required ending inventory.

---

### 1. Sets
- \(I=\{I,II,III\}\)  Products  
- \(Q=\{1,2,3,4\}\)  Quarters (planning horizon)

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Value (given) |
|--------|---------|---------------|
| \(d_{i,q}\) | Demand (contract‑booking) of product *i* in quarter *q* | 1500,1000,2000,1200 (I); 1500,1500,1200,1500 (II); 1000,2000,1500,2500 (III) |
| \(\tau_i\) | Production time (hours) required for one unit of product *i* | \(\tau_I=2,\;\tau_{II}=4,\;\tau_{III}=3\) |
| \(C^{\text{short}}_i\) | Shortage penalty per unit of product *i* | \(C^{\text{short}}_I=C^{\text{short}}_{II}=20\); \(C^{\text{short}}_{III}=10\) |
| \(C^{\text{hold}}\) | Holding cost per unit of inventory carried to the next quarter | 5 |
| \(T\) | Production‑time capacity per quarter (hours) | 15 000 |
| \(I^{\text{init}}_i\) | Initial inventory at the start of quarter 1 | 0 for all *i* |
| \(I^{\text{end}}_i\) | Required ending inventory after quarter 4 | 150 for all *i* |

### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Definition | Domain |
|--------|------------|--------|
| \(p_{i,q}\) | Units of product *i* produced in quarter *q* | \(p_{i,q}\ge 0\) |
| \(\text{inv}_{i,q}\) | Inventory of product *i* **at the end** of quarter *q* (to be carried to *q+1*) | \(\text{inv}_{i,q}\ge 0\) |
| \(s_{i,q}\) | Shortage (back‑order) of product *i* at the end of quarter *q* | \(s_{i,q}\ge 0\) |

### 4. Objective function  

\[
\min \; Z \;=\;
\sum_{q=1}^{4}\Big[
20\big(s_{I,q}+s_{II,q}\big) \;+\; 10\,s_{III,q}
\;+\; 5\sum_{i\in I}\text{inv}_{i,q}
\Big].
\]

The first two terms are shortage penalties (different for product III), the last term is the holding cost for all inventory carried forward.

### 5. Constraints  

**5.1 Inventory balance (flow)** – for every product *i* and quarter *q*  

\[
\text{inv}_{i,q}= \text{inv}_{i,q-1}+p_{i,q}-d_{i,q}+s_{i,q}\qquad
\forall i\in I,\; q=1,\dots,4,
\]
with the initial inventory condition  

\[
\text{inv}_{i,0}=I^{\text{init}}_i=0\qquad\forall i\in I .
\]

**5.2 Required ending inventory**  

\[
\text{inv}_{i,4}=I^{\text{end}}_i=150\qquad\forall i\in I .
\]

**5.3 Production‑time capacity** – each quarter cannot exceed the 15 000 h limit  

\[
\sum_{i\in I}\tau_i\,p_{i,q}\le T\qquad\forall q\in Q .
\]

**5.4 Forbidden production of product I in quarter 2**  

\[
p_{I,2}=0 .
\]

**5.5 Non‑negativity**  

\[
p_{i,q},\;\text{inv}_{i,q},\;s_{i,q}\ge 0\qquad\forall i\in I,\;q\in Q .
\]

### 6. Complete MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\; & \sum_{q=1}^{4}\Big[20\big(s_{I,q}+s_{II,q}\big)+10\,s_{III,q}+5\sum_{i\in I}\text{inv}_{i,q}\Big] \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{inv}_{i,q}= \text{inv}_{i,q-1}+p_{i,q}-d_{i,q}+s_{i,q} &&\forall i\in I,\; q=1,\dots,4,\\
& \text{inv}_{i,0}=0 &&\forall i\in I,\\
& \text{inv}_{i,4}=150 &&\forall i\in I,\\
& \sum_{i\in I}\tau_i\,p_{i,q}\le 15\,000 &&\forall q=1,\dots,4,\\
& p_{I,2}=0,\\
& p_{i,q},\;\text{inv}_{i,q},\;s_{i,q}\ge 0 &&\forall i\in I,\;q=1,\dots,4.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

**Interpretation**

- The optimal values of \(p_{i,q}\) give the production schedule for each product and quarter.  
- \(\text{inv}_{i,q}\) tells how many units are stored at the end of each quarter (incurring the $5/unit holding cost).  
- \(s_{i,q}\) indicates any unmet demand (shortage) that will be penalised ($20/unit for I & II, $10/unit for III).  

The model is linear; any LP/MILP solver (e.g., CPLEX, Gurobi, GLPK, CBC, PuLP, Pyomo) can be used to obtain the cost‑optimal production plan.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model – Production, inventory and shortage planning for Products I, II, III over four quarters**

---

### 1. Sets and indices  
*Products* \(p\in P=\{I,II,III\}\)  
*Quarters* \(t\in T=\{1,2,3,4\}\)

---

### 2. Data (parameters)  

| Symbol | Meaning | Value (from the statement) |
|--------|---------|----------------------------|
| \(D_{p,t}\) | Contracted demand (units) for product \(p\) in quarter \(t\) |  

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
      & t=1 & t=2 & t=3 & t=4\\\hline
I     &1500&1000&2000&1200\\
II    &1500&1500&1200&1500\\
III   &1000&2000&1500&2500
\end{array}
\] |
| \(c^{\text{hold}} =5\) | Holding cost $/unit/quarter (same for all products) | – |
| \(c^{\text{short}}_{I}=c^{\text{short}}_{II}=20\) | Shortage penalty $/unit/quarter for I and II | – |
| \(c^{\text{short}}_{III}=10\) | Shortage penalty $/unit/quarter for III | – |
| \(H =15000\) | Production‑hour capacity per quarter (hours) | – |
| \(h_I =2,\;h_{II}=4,\;h_{III}=3\) | Hours required to produce one unit of each product (given) | – |
| \(I^{\text{end}}_{p}=150\) | Required ending inventory (units) for each product after Q4 | – |
| \(M\) | Large constant for a “big‑M’’ formulation (e.g. \(10^6\)) | – |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{p,t}\ge 0\) | continuous | Units of product \(p\) produced in quarter \(t\) |
| \(I_{p,t}\ge 0\) | continuous | Inventory of product \(p\) **at the end** of quarter \(t\) |
| \(s_{p,t}\ge 0\) | integer (or continuous) | Shortage (unmet demand) of product \(p\) in quarter \(t\) |
| \(y\) (optional) | binary | Used only if a big‑M formulation is preferred for “no production of I in Q2’’; otherwise not needed |

---

### 4. Model formulation  

#### Objective (minimise total cost)

\[
\min \; Z \;=\;
\underbrace{\sum_{p\in P}\sum_{t\in T} c^{\text{hold}}\, I_{p,t}}_{\text{holding cost}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{p\in P}\sum_{t\in T} c^{\text{short}}_{p}\, s_{p,t}}_{\text{shortage penalty}}
\]

#### Constraints  

1. **Inventory balance (flow)** – for every product and quarter  

\[
I_{p,t-1}+x_{p,t}-s_{p,t}=D_{p,t}\qquad\forall p\in P,\;t\in T
\]

with the *virtual* initial inventory  

\[
I_{p,0}=0\qquad\forall p\in P
\]

**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model**  

The model decides which of the six children are taken on the trip.  
All data that are not given in the statement are introduced as *reasonable assumptions* and are clearly marked.

---

## 1. Sets and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Value (given) |
|--------|---------|---------------|
| \(N=\{H,\,He,\,R,\,F,\,G,\,Gi\}\) | Set of children (Harry, Hermione, Ron, Fred, George, Ginny) | – |
| \(c_H = 1200\) | Cost of taking Harry | – |
| \(c_{He}= 1650\) | Cost of taking Hermione | – |
| \(c_R = 750\)  | Cost of taking Ron | – |
| \(c_F = 800\)  | Cost of taking Fred | – |
| \(c_G = 800\)  | Cost of taking George | – |
| \(c_{Gi}=1500\) | Cost of taking Ginny (the youngest) | – |
| \(C_{\max}=4\) | Maximum number of children that may be taken | – |
| \(C_{\min}=3\) | Minimum number of children that must be taken (family decision) | – |

*Assumption*: All costs are expressed in the same monetary unit (e.g., dollars) and are additive – the total cost is the sum of the selected children’s individual costs.

---

## 2. Decision variables  

For every child \(i\in N\) we introduce a binary variable  

\[
x_i =\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if child } i \text{ is taken on the trip},\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Thus  

\[
x_H,\;x_{He},\;x_R,\;x_F,\;x_G,\;x_{Gi}\in\{0,1\}.
\]

---

## 3. Objective function  

Minimize the total monetary cost of the selected children:

\[
\boxed{\min \; Z = 1200\,x_H + 1650\,x_{He} + 750\,x_R + 800\,x_F + 800\,x_G + 1500\,x_{Gi}}
\]

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1. Mandatory inclusion of Ginny  

Ginny must be taken:

\[
x_{Gi}=1 \tag{C1}
\]

### 4.2. Cardinality limits  

Number of selected children cannot exceed the vehicle capacity and must respect the family’s decision to take at least three children:

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_H + x_{He} + x_R + x_F + x_G + x_{Gi} &\le C_{\max}=4 \tag{C2}\\
x_H + x_{He} + x_R + x_F + x_G + x_{Gi} &\ge C_{\min}=3 \tag{C3}
\end{aligned}
\]

### 4.3. Compatibility / logical relations  

The narrative gives four logical rules. They are translated into linear (big‑M) constraints.  
Because all variables are binary, the following simple “implication” forms are sufficient:

*If Harry is taken, Fred cannot be taken*  

\[
x_H + x_F \le 1 \tag{C4}
\]

*If Harry is taken, George cannot be taken*  

\[
x_H + x_G \le 1 \tag{C5}
\]

*If George is taken, Fred must also be taken*  

\[
x_G \le x_F \qquad\text{(equivalently } x_G - x_F \le 0\text{)} \tag{C6}
\]

*If George is taken, Hermione must also be taken*  

\[
x_G \le x_{He} \qquad\text{(equivalently } x_G - x_{He} \le 0\text{)} \tag{C7}
\]

These constraints enforce the required “if‑then” relationships while preserving linearity.

---

## 5. Complete MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\; & 1200\,x_H + 1650\,x_{He} + 750\,x_R + 800\,x_F + 800\,x_G + 1500\,x_{Gi} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
& x_{Gi}=1 &&\text{(C1)}\\
& x_H + x_{He} + x_R + x_F + x_G + x_{Gi} \le 4 &&\text{(C2)}\\
& x_H + x_{He} + x_R + x_F + x_G + x_{Gi} \ge 3 &&\text{(C3)}\\
& x_H + x_F \le 1 &&\text{(C4)}\\
& x_H + x_G \le 1 &&\text{(C5)}\\
& x_G - x_F \le 0 &&\text{(C6)}\\
& x_G - x_{He} \le 0 &&\text{(C7)}\\
& x_i\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall i\in N &&\text{(binary)}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. Interpretation of the solution  

Solving the above MILP (e.g., with any standard solver such as CPLEX, Gurobi, CBC, or the open‑source `PuLP`/`ortools` Python libraries) yields the set of children that minimizes total cost while respecting all family constraints.  

Because Ginny is forced in (cost = 1500) and at most three additional children can be chosen, the model will typically select the cheapest compatible children (Ron, Fred, George, etc.) unless the compatibility constraints force a more expensive combination (e.g., taking George obliges the inclusion of Fred and Hermione).  

The optimal objective value **Z\*** will be the minimum total cost achievable under the given rules.  

---  

**Assumptions made**  

1. All costs are additive and there are no discounts or economies of scale.  
2. The “maximum of 4 children” includes Ginny (i.e., the total number of children on the trip cannot exceed four).  
3. Binary variables are sufficient to model the “take / do not take” decision.  

If any of these assumptions need to be changed, the corresponding coefficients or right‑hand‑side values can be adjusted without altering the overall structure of the model.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the Vehicle‑Routing Problem with Hard Time‑Windows (VRP‑HTW)**  

The formulation below follows the classic CVRP structure and adds *hard* time‑window constraints.  
All symbols are defined in the “Sets, Parameters and Decision Variables’’ section.  
The model is completely linear, therefore it can be handed to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(N=\{0,1,\dots ,n\}\) | Set of *nodes* (0 = depot, 1…\(n\) = customers). |
| \(V=N\setminus\{0\}\) | Set of customers only. |
| \(K=\{1,\dots ,m\}\) | Set of identical vehicles (maximum fleet size \(m\)). |
| \(A=\{(i,j)\mid i\neq j,\; i,j\in N\}\) | Set of directed arcs (possible travel from *i* to *j*). |

*Assumption*: All vehicles start and end at the depot (node 0) and have the same capacity \(Q\).  
If the fleet size is not known a priori, a sufficiently large \(m\) can be used together with a “vehicle‑used’’ binary variable (see § 3).

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical unit |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| \(c_{ij}\) | Travel cost (or distance, time) from node *i* to node *j*. | km / $ |
| \(d_i\) | Demand of customer *i* (amount of goods that must be delivered). | units |
| \(Q\) | Vehicle capacity (maximum total demand a vehicle can carry). | units |
| \([e_i,\,l_i]\) | **Hard** time‑window of customer *i*: service may start only after \(e_i\) and must start no later than \(l_i\). | minutes |
| \(s_i\) | Service time at customer *i* (time needed to unload/load). | minutes |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant, larger than any feasible arrival time (e.g. \(M = \max_i l_i + \sum_{i} s_i + \max_{i,j} c_{ij}\)). | minutes |
| \(T_{\max}\) | Maximum route duration allowed for a vehicle (optional, can be set to a large number). | minutes |

*Assumption*: The depot (node 0) has a time‑window \([e_0,l_0]\) that is wide enough to contain the whole planning horizon (e.g. \([0,T_{\max}]\)).  

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \(x_{ij}^k \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if vehicle \(k\) travels directly from node *i* to node *j*; 0 otherwise. |
| \(u_i^k \ge 0\) | continuous | **Arrival time** of vehicle \(k\) at node *i* (the instant service starts). |
| \(q_i^k \ge 0\) | continuous | **Load** of vehicle \(k\) after leaving node *i* (cumulative demand already served). |
| \(y_k \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if vehicle \(k\) is used (departs from the depot at least once). |

*Assumption*: The model uses the “flow‑based’’ representation; subtour elimination is achieved with the classic MTZ (Miller‑Tucker‑Zemlin) auxiliary variables \(q_i^k\) (load) and the time‑variables \(u_i^k\).  

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

The most common objective for a VRP‑HTW is **minimising total travelled distance (or cost)**:

\[
\boxed{\min\; \sum_{k\in K}\;\sum_{(i,j)\in A}\; c_{ij}\; x_{ij}^k}
\]

If the planner also wants to minimise the number of vehicles, the term \(\sum_{k} y_k\) can be added with a weight \(\lambda\):

\[
\min\; \sum_{k\in K}\;\sum_{(i,j)\in A} c_{ij} x_{ij}^k \;+\; \lambda\;\sum_{k\in K} y_k .
\]

(Here \(\lambda\) is a large constant that forces the solver to use as few vehicles as possible without sacrificing feasibility.)

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1  Each customer is visited exactly once  

\[
\sum_{k\in K}\;\sum_{j\in N\setminus\{i\}} x_{ij}^k \;=\; 1 \qquad \forall i\in V
\tag{C1}
\]

### 5.2  Flow conservation for each vehicle  

*Depot departure*  

\[
\sum_{j\in N\setminus\{0\}} x_{0j}^k \;=\; y_k \qquad \forall k\in K
\tag{C2}
\]

*Depot return*  

\[
\sum_{i\in N\setminus\{0\}} x_{i0}^k \;=\; y_k \qquad \forall k\in K
\tag{C3}
\]

*Intermediate nodes*  

\[
\sum_{j\in N\setminus\{i\}} x_{ij}^k \;-\; \sum_{j\in N\setminus\{i\}} x_{ji}^k \;=\; 0 
\qquad \forall k\in K,\; \forall i\in V
\tag{C4}
\]

These constraints guarantee that each vehicle that arrives at a customer also leaves it (except the depot).

### 5.3  Vehicle capacity (load) propagation (MTZ‑style)  

\[
q_j^k \;\ge\; q_i^k + d_j - Q\,(1-x_{ij}^k) \qquad 
\forall k\in K,\; \forall (i,j)\in A,\; i\neq 0
\tag{C5}
\]

\[
0 \le q_i^k \le Q \qquad \forall k\in K,\; \forall i\in N
\tag{C6}
\]

\[
q_0^k = 0 \qquad \forall k\in K
\tag{C7}
\]

Interpretation: when arc \((i,j)\) is used by vehicle \(k\), the load after visiting *j* equals the load after *i* plus the demand of *j*. The big‑\(M\) term \(Q\,(1-x_{ij}^k)\) de‑activates the constraint when the arc is not used.

### 5.4  Hard time‑window feasibility  

*Arrival after the opening of the window*  

\[
u_i^k \;\ge\; e_i \qquad \forall k\in K,\; \forall i\in V
\tag{C8}
\]

*Arrival before the closing of the window*  

\[
u_i^k \;\le\; l_i \qquad \forall k\in K,\; \forall i\in V
\tag{C9}
\]

*Time propagation along a used arc*  

\[
u_j^k \;\ge\; u_i^k + s_i + c_{ij} - M\,(1-x_{ij}^k) 
\qquad \forall k\in K,\; \forall (i,j)\in A
\tag{C10}
\]

If arc \((i,j)\) is traversed, the service at *j* can start only after the service at *i* finishes (arrival time + service time) plus travel time. The big‑\(M\) term relaxes the inequality when the arc is not used.

*Depot time* (optional, usually not binding)  

\[
u_0^k = 0 \qquad \forall k\in K
\tag{C11}
\]

### 5.5  Optional route‑duration limit  

\[
u_0^k + \sum_{(i,j)\in A} c_{ij} x_{ij}^k \;\le\; T_{\max} \qquad \forall k\in K
\tag{C12}
\]

(This guarantees that the total time a vehicle spends on the route does not exceed a planning horizon.)

### 5.6  Binary and non‑negativity  

\[
x_{ij}^k \in \{0,1\} \qquad \forall k\in K,\; (i,j)\in A
\tag{C13}
\]

\[
y_k \in \{0,1\} \qquad \forall k\in K
\tag{C14}
\]

\[
u_i^k \ge 0,\; q_i^k \ge 0 \qquad \forall k\in K,\; i\in N
\tag{C15}
\]

---

## 6.  Complete MILP model  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{k\in K}\;\sum_{(i,j)\in A} c_{ij}\,x_{ij}^k 
\;+\; \lambda\!\sum_{k\in K} y_k \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(C1)–(C15)} \\
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities are the products of a binary variable with a constant (the big‑\(M\) terms), which are perfectly admissible in a MILP.

---

## 7.  Remarks & Modelling Choices  

1. **Big‑M value** – Choose the smallest possible value to improve numerical stability. A safe bound is  
   \[
   M = \max_{i\in V} l_i \;+\; \max_{i\in V} s_i \;+\; \max_{(i,j)\in A} c_{ij}.
   \]

2. **Vehicle fleet size** – If the exact number of vehicles is unknown, set \(m\) to a large number (e.g. \(m=n\)) and let the objective penalise each used vehicle through \(\lambda\).  

3. **Alternative subtour elimination** – Instead of the MTZ load variables \(q_i^k\), a *flow* formulation (using additional continuous variables \(\pi_i^k\) that represent the position of node *i* in vehicle \(k\)’s route) can be used. The presented MTZ version is compact and linear.

4. **Multiple depots / heterogeneous fleet** – The model can be extended by adding a depot index \(d\) and vehicle‑type parameters \(Q_k,\,c_{ij}^k\).  

5. **Data example** – The block you supplied (`r101.txt`) contains, for each node *i*:  
   - coordinates (x, y) – can be turned into Euclidean distances for \(c_{ij}\);  
   - demand (the 4th column);  
   - time‑window start \(e_i\) (5th column) and end \(l_i\) (6th column);  
   - service time (7th column).  

   Using those columns, the parameters above can be populated directly.

---

### 8.  Summary  

The formulation above completely describes the **Vehicle‑Routing Problem with Hard Time‑Windows (VRP‑HTW)** as a mixed‑integer linear program.  

*Decision variables* decide which arcs each vehicle traverses, when each vehicle arrives at each node, and how much load it carries.  

*Constraints* enforce:  

* each customer is served exactly once,  
* flow conservation for every vehicle,  
* vehicle‑capacity limits,  
* hard time‑window feasibility (no early/late service allowed),  
* optional limits on total route duration and on the number of vehicles used.  

The *objective* minimises total travel cost (or distance) and, optionally, the number of used vehicles.  

All elements are linear; therefore any modern MILP solver can be used to obtain optimal routes that respect the hard time‑windows.

**Variables**

* \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if a vehicle travels directly from node \(i\) to node \(j\) ( \(i\neq j\) , \(i,j\in N=\{0,\dots ,n\}\) ; node 0 is the depot).  
* \(u_i\ge 0\) – arrival time of the vehicle at node \(i\).  
* \(\ell_i\ge 0\) – load of the vehicle after leaving node \(i\) ( \(\ell_0=0\) ).  

**Parameters**

* \(c_{ij}\) – travel cost (or distance) from \(i\) to \(j\).  
* \(t_{ij}\) – travel time from \(i\) to \(j\) (often proportional to \(c_{ij}\)).  
* \(d_i\) – demand of customer \(i\) ( \(d_0=0\) ).  
* \(Q\) – vehicle capacity (identical fleet).  
* \([e_i,l_i]\) – hard time‑window of node \(i\) ( \(e_0=0,\;l_0\) large).  
* \(s_i\) – service time at node \(i\) ( \(s_0=0\) ).  
* \(K\) – number of vehicles used (can be fixed or minimised).  
* \(M\) – a sufficiently large constant, e.g.  
  \[
  M=\max_{i\in N}l_i+\max_{i,j\in N}t_{ij}.
  \]  
* \(\varepsilon\) – a tiny positive number (e.g., \(10^{-4}\)) for strict MTZ ordering.

**Objective**

\[
\min\; \sum_{i\in N}\sum_{j\in N\setminus\{i\}} c_{ij}\,x_{ij}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

**Constraints**

1. **Each customer is left exactly once**  
   \[
   \sum_{j\in N\setminus\{i\}} x_{ij}=1 \qquad\forall i\in N\setminus\{0\}
   \tag{C1}
   \]

2. **Each customer is entered exactly once**  
   \[
   \sum_{i\in N\setminus\{j\}} x_{ij}=1 \qquad\forall j\in N\setminus\{0\}
   \tag{C2}
   \]

3. **Depot departure and return** (if \(K\) is fixed)  
   \[
   \sum_{j\in N\setminus\{0\}} x_{0j}=K,\qquad
   \sum_{i\in N\setminus\{0\}} x_{i0}=K
   \tag{C3}
   \]

4. **Time‑propagation with waiting (big‑M)**  
   \[
   u_j\;\ge\; u_i + s_i + t_{ij} - M\,(1-x_{ij})
   \qquad\forall i\neq j,\; i,j\in N
   \tag{C4}
   \]

5. **Hard time windows**  
   \[
   e_i\le u_i\le l_i \qquad\forall i\in N\setminus\{0\}
   \tag{C5}
   \]

6. **Load propagation**  
   \[
   \ell_j\;\ge\; \ell_i + d_j - Q\,(1-x_{ij})
   \qquad\forall i\neq j,\; i,j\in N
   \tag{C6}
   \]

7. **Load limits**  
   \[
   0\le \ell_i\le Q \qquad\forall i\in N\setminus\{0\}
   \tag{C7}
   \]

8. **Depot initial conditions**  
   \[
   \ell_0=0,\qquad u_0=0
   \tag{C8}
   \]

9. **MTZ subtour‑elimination (ordering of visits)**  
   \[
   u_i - u_j + M\,x_{ij}\;\le\; M-\varepsilon
   \qquad\forall i\neq j,\; i,j\in N\setminus\{0\}
   \tag{C9}
   \]

10. **Binary and non‑negativity**  
    \[
    x_{ij}\in\{0,1\},\; u_i\ge0,\; \ell_i\ge0\qquad\forall i,j\in N.
    \tag{C10}
    \]

---

### Assumptions (explicit)

* All vehicles are identical with capacity \(Q\).  
* Travel time \(t_{ij}\) is known for every ordered pair \((i,j)\).  
* Service times \(s_i\) are deterministic and known.  
* The big‑\(M\) constant is chosen large enough to deactivate time‑propagation when an arc is not used.  
* If the number of vehicles is not predetermined, one may replace constraints (C3) by a set of binary vehicle‑usage variables and minimise \(\sum_k y_k\).  

The model above fully describes the **Vehicle Routing Problem with Hard Time Windows (VRP‑HTW)** as a mixed‑integer linear program.

Text:
**MILP model for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Hard Time‑Windows (VRP‑HTW)**  

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(V=\{0,1,\dots ,n\}\) | Nodes (0 = depot, 1…n = customers) |
| \(C=\{1,\dots ,n\}\) | Set of customers |
| \(K=\{1,\dots ,K_{\max}\}\) | Set of identical vehicles (upper bound on number of routes) |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \(d_{ij}\) | Distance (or travel cost) from node \(i\) to node \(j\) (symmetric) | km |
| \(t_{ij}\) | Travel time from \(i\) to \(j\) (often proportional to \(d_{ij}\) ) | min |
| \(s_i\) | Service time at node \(i\) ( \(s_0=0\) ) | min |
| \(q_i\) | Demand of customer \(i\) ( \(q_0=0\) ) | load units |
| \(Q\) | Vehicle capacity | load units |
| \([a_i,b_i]\) | Hard time‑window for node \(i\) (arrival must satisfy \(a_i\le t_i\le b_i\) ) | min |
| \(M\) | Large constant > \(\max_i b_i+\max_{i,j} t_{ij}\) (for time constraints) | min |
| \(M_Q\) | Large constant ≥ \(Q\) (for capacity constraints) | load units |
| \(|C|\) | Number of customers (= \(n\)) | – |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Definition |
|--------|------|------------|
| \(x_{ijk}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if vehicle \(k\) travels directly from node \(i\) to node \(j\) |
| \(t_{ik}\ge0\) | continuous | Arrival time of vehicle \(k\) at node \(i\) |
| \(l_{ik}\ge0\) | continuous | Load of vehicle \(k\) **upon arrival** at node \(i\) (after serving \(i\)) |
| \(u_{ik}\ge0\) | continuous | MTZ auxiliary variable (order of node \(i\) in vehicle \(k\)’s tour) |
| (optional) \(y_k\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if vehicle \(k\) is used (needed only to limit the number of active vehicles) |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{\min\; \sum_{k\in K}\;\sum_{i\in V}\;\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}} d_{ij}\,x_{ijk}}
\]

(minimise total travelled distance; replace \(d_{ij}\) by \(t_{ij}\) if minimising total time)

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Customer service  
\[
\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}} x_{ijk}=1 \qquad\forall i\in C \tag{C1}
\]
\[
\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{i\in V\setminus\{j\}} x_{ijk}=1 \qquad\forall j\in C \tag{C2}
\]

#### 5.2 Depot start / end (vehicles may stay idle)  
\[
\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{0\}} x_{0jk}\le 1 \qquad\forall k\in K \tag{C3}
\]
\[
\sum_{i\in V\setminus\{0\}} x_{i0k}\le 1 \qquad\forall k\in K \tag{C4}
\]

#### 5.3 Flow conservation (if a vehicle enters a node it must leave)  
\[
\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}} x_{ijk}= \sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}} x_{jik}
\qquad\forall i\in V,\;\forall k\in K \tag{C5}
\]

#### 5.4 Capacity propagation (big‑M linearisation)  
\[
l_{jk}\ge l_{ik}+q_j-M_Q\,(1-x_{ijk}) \qquad\forall i,j\in V,\;i\neq j,\;k\in K \tag{C6a}
\]
\[
l_{jk}\le l_{ik}+q_j+M_Q\,(1-x_{ijk}) \qquad\forall i,j\in V,\;i\neq j,\;k\in K \tag{C6b}
\]

#### 5.5 Load limits and depot initialisation  
\[
0\le l_{ik}\le Q \qquad\forall i\in V,\;k\in K \tag{C7}
\]
\[
l_{0k}=0 \qquad\forall k\in K \tag{C8}
\]

#### 5.6 Time‑window propagation (big‑M)  
\[
t_{jk}\ge t_{ik}+s_i+t_{ij}-M\,(1-x_{ijk}) \qquad\forall i,j\in V,\;i\neq j,\;k\in K \tag{C9}
\]

#### 5.7 Hard time‑windows (waiting allowed)  
\[
a_i\le t_{ik}\le b_i \qquad\forall i\in V,\;k\in K \tag{C10}
\]

#### 5.8 MTZ subtour‑elimination  
\[
1\le u_{ik}\le |C| \qquad\forall i\in C,\;k\in K \tag{C11}
\]
\[
u_{0k}=0 \qquad\forall k\in K \tag{C12}
\]
\[
u_{ik}-u_{jk}+|C|\,x_{ijk}\le |C|-1 \qquad\forall i,j\in C,\;i\neq j,\;k\in K \tag{C13}
\]

#### 5.9 (Optional) Vehicle‑activation linking and limit on number of used vehicles  
\[
\sum_{j\neq0} x_{0jk}=y_k \qquad\forall k\in K \tag{C14}
\]
\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_k\le K_{\max} \tag{C15}
\]

If the set \(K\) already contains exactly \(K_{\max}\) vehicles, constraints (C14)–(C15) can be omitted.

---

### 6. Complete MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{i\in V}\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}} d_{ij}\,x_{ijk}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. }&
\text{(C1)–(C15)}\\[1mm]
&x_{ijk}\in\{0,1\},\;t_{ik}\ge0,\;l_{ik}\ge0,\;u_{ik}\ge0\quad\forall i,j\in V,\;k\in K.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are the routing binaries \(x_{ijk}\) (and optionally the vehicle‑activation binaries \(y_k\)). The model therefore belongs to the class of **Mixed‑Integer Linear Programs (MILP)** and can be solved with any standard MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Hard Time‑Windows (VRP‑HTW)**  

The formulation below describes a single‑depot, homogeneous‑fleet VRP in which every customer must be served exactly once, each vehicle respects a capacity limit, and service at every customer must start inside a hard time‑window \([a_i ,b_i]\). The objective is to minimise the total travelled distance (or cost).  

---

### 1. Sets, parameters and indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(V=\{0,1,\dots ,n\}\) | Set of nodes; node 0 is the depot, \(i=1,\dots ,n\) are customers |
| \(K=\{1,\dots ,m\}\) | Set of identical vehicles (fleet size) |
| \(c_{ij}\) | Travel distance (or cost) from node \(i\) to node \(j\) (non‑negative) |
| \(d_i\) | Demand of customer \(i\) ( \(d_0=0\) ) |
| \(Q\) | Capacity of each vehicle (identical) |
| \([a_i ,b_i]\) | Hard time‑window for node \(i\) (arrival must satisfy \(a_i\le t_i\le b_i\)); for the depot set \(a_0=0,\;b_0\) large |
| \(s_i\) | Service time at node \(i\) (time needed to load/unload) |
| \(M\) | A sufficiently large constant (big‑M), e.g. \(M=\max_i b_i+\max_{i,j}c_{ij}\) |
| \(n\) | Number of customers ( \(|V|=n+1\) ) |

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| \(x_{ij}^{k}\) | Binary \(\{0,1\}\) | 1 if vehicle \(k\) traverses the directed arc \((i,j)\); 0 otherwise |
| \(t_i^{k}\) | Continuous \(\ge 0\) | Arrival (start‑of‑service) time of vehicle \(k\) at node \(i\) |
| \(q_i^{k}\) | Continuous \(\ge 0\) | Load of vehicle \(k\) **after** serving node \(i\) (i.e. when leaving \(i\)) |
| \(u_i^{k}\) | Continuous \(\ge 0\) | MTZ auxiliary variable (position of node \(i\) in the route of vehicle \(k\)) |

---

### 3. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{\min \; \sum_{k\in K}\;\sum_{i\in V}\;\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}} c_{ij}\;x_{ij}^{k}}
\]

The sum adds the travel distance of every arc that is used by any vehicle.

---

### 4. Constraints  

#### 4.1. Customer‑service constraints  

*Each customer is entered exactly once*  

\[
\sum_{k\in K}\;\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}} x_{ij}^{k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in V\setminus\{0\}\tag{C1}
\]

*Each customer is left exactly once*  

\[
\sum_{k\in K}\;\sum_{i\in V\setminus\{j\}} x_{ij}^{k}=1 \qquad\forall j\in V\setminus\{0\}\tag{C2}
\]

#### 4.2. Depot degree (each vehicle starts and ends at the depot)  

\[
\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{0\}} x_{0j}^{k}=1 \qquad\forall k\in K \tag{C3}
\]

\[
\sum_{i\in V\setminus\{0\}} x_{i0}^{k}=1 \qquad\forall k\in K \tag{C4}
\]

#### 4.3. Flow conservation for every vehicle  

\[
\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}} x_{ij}^{k}= \sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}} x_{ji}^{k}\qquad\forall i\in V\setminus\{0\},\;k\in K \tag{C5}
\]

#### 4.4. Vehicle capacity (load propagation)  

Load at the depot is zero  

\[
q_{0}^{k}=0 \qquad\forall k\in K \tag{C6}
\]

Load update when an arc is used  

\[
q_{j}^{k}\ge q_{i}^{k}+d_{j}-Q\,(1-x_{ij}^{k})\qquad\forall i\in V,\;j\in V\setminus\{i\},\;k\in K \tag{C7}
\]

Capacity bound  

\[
0\le q_{i}^{k}\le Q \qquad\forall i\in V,\;k\in K \tag{C8}
\]

#### 4.5. Hard time‑window constraints  

Depot start time (optional)  

\[
t_{0}^{k}=0 \qquad\forall k\in K \tag{C9}
\]

Time‑window enforcement  

\[
a_i\le t_{i}^{k}\le b_i \qquad\forall i\in V,\;k\in K \tag{C10}
\]

Time propagation along a used arc (service time \(s_i\) is added before travelling)  

\[
t_{j}^{k}\ge t_{i}^{k}+s_i+c_{ij}-M\,(1-x_{ij}^{k})\qquad\forall i\in V,\;j\in V\setminus\{i\},\;k\in K \tag{C11}
\]

#### 4.6. Sub‑tour elimination (MTZ formulation)  

Fix the depot position  

\[
u_{0}^{k}=0 \qquad\forall k\in K \tag{C12}
\]

Ordering constraints for every pair of distinct nodes  

\[
u_{j}^{k}\ge u_{i}^{k}+1-(n+1)\,(1-x_{ij}^{k})\qquad\forall i\in V,\;j\in V\setminus\{i\},\;k\in K \tag{C13}
\]

Bounds on the MTZ variables  

\[
0\le u_{i}^{k}\le n \qquad\forall i\in V,\;k\in K \tag{C14}
\]

These constraints force a consistent increasing “position’’ along each vehicle’s route; any closed sub‑tour that does **not** contain the depot would violate (C13) and is therefore eliminated.

#### 4.7. Variable domains  

\[
x_{ij}^{k}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall i\neq j,\;i,j\in V,\;k\in K
\]

\[
t_{i}^{k}\ge 0,\; q_{i}^{k}\ge 0,\; u_{i}^{k}\ge 0\qquad\forall i\in V,\;k\in K
\]

---

### 5. Complete MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{i\in V}\sum_{j\in V\setminus\{i\}} c_{ij}\,x_{ij}^{k}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &\text{(C1)–(C14)}\\[2pt]
&x_{ij}^{k}\in\{0,1\},\;t_{i}^{k}\ge0,\;q_{i}^{k}\ge0,\;u_{i}^{k}\ge0\qquad\forall i,j,k .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6. Remarks  

* **Binary variables \(x_{ij}^{k}\)** encode the routing decisions.  
* **Arrival‑time variables \(t_i^{k}\)** guarantee that every service starts inside its hard time‑window.  
* **Load variables \(q_i^{k}\)** enforce the vehicle‑capacity limit.  
* **MTZ variables \(u_i^{k}\)** provide a linear way to forbid subtours that do not contain the depot.  
* The model is **linear** (all constraints are linear) and contains only the binary routing variables as integer decisions, making it suitable for any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (CBC, GLPK) MILP solver.

Solving this MILP yields the optimal set of vehicle routes, their schedules, and loads while minimising total travel distance and respecting all hard time‑window constraints.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model**

The model decides how many grams of each vegetable to buy and which animal protein to select in order to **maximise total dietary fibre** while respecting a budget, a total‑weight requirement and the rule that at least two different vegetables must be used.

---

### 1. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| `g_okra`      | continuous, ≥ 0 | grams of okra purchased |
| `g_carrot`    | continuous, ≥ 0 | grams of carrots purchased |
| `g_celery`    | continuous, ≥ 0 | grams of celery purchased |
| `g_cabbage`   | continuous, ≥ 0 | grams of cabbage purchased |
| `y_okra`      | binary (0/1)    | 1 if any okra is bought, 0 otherwise |
| `y_carrot`    | binary (0/1)    | 1 if any carrots are bought, 0 otherwise |
| `y_celery`    | binary (0/1)    | 1 if any celery is bought, 0 otherwise |
| `y_cabbage`   | binary (0/1)    | 1 if any cabbage is bought, 0 otherwise |
| `z_salmon`    | binary (0/1)    | 1 if salmon is chosen as the protein, 0 otherwise |
| `z_beef`      | binary (0/1)    | 1 if beef is chosen as the protein, 0 otherwise |
| `z_pork`      | binary (0/1)    | 1 if pork is chosen as the protein, 0 otherwise |

Only one protein may be selected (`z_salmon + z_beef + z_pork = 1`).  
A vegetable is “selected’’ when its binary `y` is 1; the linking constraints force its gram amount to zero otherwise.

---

### 2. Data (price per gram, fibre per gram)

| Item      | Price (\$/g) | Fibre (g / g) |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|
| Okra      | 0.026 / 100 g = **0.026** | 3.2 g / 100 g = **0.032** |
| Carrot    | 0.012 / 100 g = **0.012** | 2.7 g / 100 g = **0.027** |
| Celery    | 0.016 / 100 g = **0.016** | 1.6 g / 100 g = **0.016** |
| Cabbage   | 0.023 / 100 g = **0.023** | 2.0 g / 100 g = **0.020** |
| Salmon    | 4 / 100 g = **0.040** | – |
| Beef      | 3.6 / 100 g = **0.036** | – |
| Pork      | 1.8 / 100 g = **0.018** | – |

*(Prices are expressed per gram; fibre values are grams of fibre per gram of vegetable.)*  

*Assumption:* the protein portion contributes **100 g** to the total weight (its exact weight can be changed by multiplying the binary variable by the desired gram amount).

---

### 3. Objective function  

\[
\max\; \text{Fibre}=0.032\,g_{\text{okra}}+0.027\,g_{\text{carrot}}+0.016\,g_{\text{celery}}+0.020\,g_{\text{cabbage}}
\]

Only vegetables provide fibre.

---

### 4. Constraints  

**Budget**

\[
0.026\,g_{\text{okra}}+0.012\,g_{\text{carrot}}+0.016\,g_{\text{celery}}+0.023\,g_{\text{cabbage}}
+0.040\,z_{\text{salmon}}+0.036\,z_{\text{beef}}+0.018\,z_{\text{pork}}\le 15
\]

**Total weight (600 g)**  

\[
g_{\text{okra}}+g_{\text{carrot}}+g_{\text{celery}}+g_{\text{cabbage}}
+100\,(z_{\text{salmon}}+z_{\text{beef}}+z_{\text{pork}})=600
\]

*(If a different protein amount is required, replace the coefficient 100 by the desired gram amount.)*

**Linking grams to selection binaries**

\[
\begin{aligned}
g_{\text{okra}}   &\le 600\,y_{\text{okra}}\\
g_{\text{carrot}} &\le 600\,y_{\text{carrot}}\\
g_{\text{celery}} &\le 600\,y_{\text{celery}}\\
g_{\text{cabbage}}&\le 600\,y_{\text{cabbage}}
\end{aligned}
\]

**At least two vegetable types**

\[
y_{\text{okra}}+y_{\text{carrot}}+y_{\text{celery}}+y_{\text{cabbage}}\ge 2
\]

**Exactly one protein choice**

\[
z_{\text{salmon}}+z_{\text{beef}}+z_{\text{pork}}=1
\]

**Non‑negativity / binary restrictions**

\[
g_{\text{okra}},g_{\text{carrot}},g_{\text{celery}},g_{\text{cabbage}}\ge0
\]
\[
y_{\text{okra}},y_{\text{carrot}},y_{\text{celery}},y_{\text{cabbage}}\in\{0,1\}
\]
\[
z_{\text{salmon}},z_{\text{beef}},z_{\text{pork}}\in\{0,1\}
\]

---

### 5. Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max\;&0.032\,g_{\text{okra}}+0.027\,g_{\text{carrot}}+0.016\,g_{\text{celery}}+0.020\,g_{\text{cabbage}}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. }&
0.026\,g_{\text{okra}}+0.012\,g_{\text{carrot}}+0.016\,g_{\text{celery}}+0.023\,g_{\text{cabbage}}\\
&\qquad+0.040\,z_{\text{salmon}}+0.036\,z_{\text{beef}}+0.018\,z_{\text{pork}}\le 15\\[4pt]
&g_{\text{okra}}+g_{\text{carrot}}+g_{\text{celery}}+g_{\text{cabbage}}\\
&\qquad+100\,(z_{\text{salmon}}+z_{\text{beef}}+z_{\text{pork}})=600\\[4pt]
&g_{\text{okra}}\le 600\,y_{\text{okra}}\\
&g_{\text{carrot}}\le 600\,y_{\text{carrot}}\\
&g_{\text{celery}}\le 600\,y_{\text{celery}}\\
&g_{\text{cabbage}}\le 600\,y_{\text{cabbage}}\\[4pt]
&y_{\text{okra}}+y_{\text{carrot}}+y_{\text{celery}}+y_{\text{cabbage}}\ge 2\\[4pt]

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model**

The model decides how many *100 g portions* of a single protein source (salmon, beef or pork) and of several vegetables (okra, carrots, celery, cabbage) Mary should buy so that the total dietary‑fiber intake is maximised while respecting a budget, a total‑weight limit and the “at least two vegetables’’ rule.

---

### 1. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning (per 100 g) |
|--------|------|----------------------|
| \(x_{\text{salmon}}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | 100 g units of salmon |
| \(x_{\text{beef}}\)    | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | 100 g units of beef |
| \(x_{\text{pork}}\)    | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | 100 g units of pork |
| \(v_{\text{okra}}\)    | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | 100 g units of okra |
| \(v_{\text{carrot}}\)  | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | 100 g units of carrots |
| \(v_{\text{celery}}\)  | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | 100 g units of celery |
| \(v_{\text{cabbage}}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | 100 g units of cabbage |
| \(y_{\text{okra}}\)    | binary (0‑1) | 1 if okra is used, 0 otherwise |
| \(y_{\text{carrot}}\)  | binary (0‑1) | 1 if carrots are used, 0 otherwise |
| \(y_{\text{celery}}\)  | binary (0‑1) | 1 if celery is used, 0 otherwise |
| \(y_{\text{cabbage}}\) | binary (0‑1) | 1 if cabbage is used, 0 otherwise |

All continuous variables are measured in **hundreds of grams** (so a value of 1 = 100 g).

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Parameter | Value | Interpretation |
|-----------|-------|----------------|
| \(c_{\text{okra}} = 3.2\) | fiber (g) per 100 g |
| \(c_{\text{carrot}} = 2.7\) | fiber (g) per 100 g |
| \(c_{\text{celery}} = 1.6\) | fiber (g) per 100 g |
| \(c_{\text{cabbage}} = 2.0\) | fiber (g) per 100 g |
| \(\text{price}_{\text{salmon}} = 4.0\) | $ per 100 g |
| \(\text{price}_{\text{beef}}   = 3.6\) | $ per 100 g |
| \(\text{price}_{\text{pork}}   = 1.8\) | $ per 100 g |
| \(\text{price}_{\text{okra}}   = 2.6\) | $ per 100 g |
| \(\text{price}_{\text{carrot}} = 1.2\) | $ per 100 g |
| \(\text{price}_{\text{celery}} = 1.6\) | $ per 100 g |
| \(\text{price}_{\text{cabbage}}= 2.3\) | $ per 100 g |
| \(\text{budget}=15\) | total money available |
| \(\text{totalWeight}=6\) | 600 g expressed in 100 g units |
| \(M=6\) | big‑M (cannot exceed total weight) |

---

### 3. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{\max \; 3.2\,v_{\text{okra}} + 2.7\,v_{\text{carrot}} + 1.6\,v_{\text{celery}} + 2.0\,v_{\text{cabbage}}}
\]

The linear combination gives the total dietary‑fiber (grams) contributed by the chosen vegetables.

---

### 4. Constraints  

1. **Budget**  
   \[
   4.0\,x_{\text{salmon}} + 3.6\,x_{\text{beef}} + 1.8\,x_{\text{pork}}
   + 2.6\,v_{\text{okra}} + 1.2\,v_{\text{carrot}} + 1.6\,v_{\text{celery}} + 2.3\,v_{\text{cabbage}}
   \le 15
   \]

2. **Total weight (600 g)**  
   \[
   x_{\text{salmon}} + x_{\text{beef}} + x_{\text{pork}}
   + v_{\text{okra}} + v_{\text{carrot}} + v_{\text{celery}} + v_{\text{cabbage}}
   = 6
   \]

3. **Exactly one protein source**  
   \[
   x_{\text{salmon}} + x_{\text{beef}} + x_{\text{pork}} = 1
   \]

4. **At least two vegetables**  
   \[
   y_{\text{okra}} + y_{\text{carrot}} + y_{\text{celery}} + y_{\text{cabbage}} \ge 2
   \]

5. **Linking (big‑M) constraints** – a vegetable can have a positive amount only if it is selected:  
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   v_{\text{okra}}   &\le M\,y_{\text{okra}}   \\
   v_{\text{carrot}} &\le M\,y_{\text{carrot}} \\
   v_{\text{celery}} &\le M\,y_{\text{celery}} \\
   v_{\text{cabbage}}&\le M\,y_{\text{cabbage}}
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad (M=6)
   \]

6. **Non‑negativity**  
   \[
   x_{\text{salmon}},\,x_{\text{beef}},\,x_{\text{pork}},\,
   v_{\text{okra}},\,v_{\text{carrot}},\,v_{\text{celery}},\,v_{\text{cabbage}} \ge 0
   \]

7. **Binary variables**  
   \[
   y_{\text{okra}},\,y_{\text{carrot}},\,y_{\text{celery}},\,y_{\text{cabbage}} \in \{0,1\}
   \]

---

### 5. Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max\;& 3.2\,v_{\text{okra}} + 2.7\,v_{\text{carrot}} + 1.6\,v_{\text{celery}} + 2.0\,v_{\text{cabbage}} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
4.0\,x_{\text{salmon}} + 3.6\,x_{\text{beef}} + 1.8\,x_{\text{pork}}
+ 2.6\,v_{\text{okra}} + 1.2\,v_{\text{carrot}} + 1.6\,v_{\text{celery}} + 2.3\,v_{\text{cabbage}} \le 15 \\[2pt]
& x_{\text{salmon}} + x_{\text{beef}} + x_{\text{pork}}
+ v_{\text{okra}} + v_{\text{carrot}} + v_{\text{celery}} + v_{\text{cabbage}} = 6 \\[2pt]
& x_{\text{salmon}} + x_{\text{beef}} + x_{\text{pork}} = 1 \\[2pt]
& y_{\text{okra}} + y_{\text{carrot}} + y_{\text{celery}} + y_{\text{cabbage}} \ge 2 \\[2pt]
& v_{\text{okra}}   \le 6\,y_{\text{okra}}   \\
& v_{\text{carrot}} \le 6\,y_{\text{carrot}} \\
& v_{\text{celery}} \le 6\,y_{\text{celery}} \\
& v_{\text{cabbage}}\le 6\,y_{\text{cabbage}} \\[2pt]
& x_{\text{salmon}},\,x_{\text{beef}},\,x_{\text{pork}},\,
   v_{\text{okra}},\,v_{\text{carrot}},\,v_{\text{celery}},\,v_{\text{cabbage}} \ge 0 \\[2pt]
& y_{\text{okra}},\,y_{\text{carrot}},\,y_{\text{celery}},\,y_{\text{cabbage}} \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6. Remarks  

* **Protein choice** – Constraint 3 forces the sum of the three protein variables to be exactly 1 (i.e., 100 g). Because they are non‑negative, this means exactly one of them will be 1 and the others 0, satisfying “choose one protein source.’’  
* **Vegetable diversity** – The binary variables together with the linking constraints guarantee that a vegetable contributes weight only if it is selected, and the sum of the binaries must be at least 2.  
* **Objective** – Maximising the weighted sum of vegetable quantities pushes the solution toward the vegetables with the highest fiber per 100 g, limited by the budget, total weight and the requirement to use at least two different vegetables.  

The presented MILP is complete and ready for solution with any standard optimizer (CPLEX, Gurobi, CBC, GLPK, etc.).

Text:
**Linear (mixed‑integer) model for the “100 000 yuan – three‑year horizon” investment problem**  

Below is a complete formulation that can be entered directly into any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, GLPK, …).  
All symbols, sets, parameters and assumptions are listed first, followed by the decision variables, the objective function and the constraints.

---

## 1.  Sets and indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(t\) | Investment **start‑period** (year) – \(t\in\{0,1,2\}\). The planning horizon ends at the end of year 3. |
| \(k\) | Investment **type** – \(k=1\) for the *one‑year* product, \(k=2\) for the *two‑year* product. |
| \(T_k\) | Set of admissible start‑periods for product \(k\) (see Assumption A2). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Value / description | Units |
|--------|---------------------|-------|
| \(B\) | Total cash available at the beginning (year 0) | 100 000 yuan |
| \(r_1\) | Return per yuan for the one‑year product (profit after 1 year) | 0.7 yuan/yuan |
| \(r_2\) | Return per yuan for the two‑year product (profit after 2 years) | 2 yuan/yuan |
| \(L\) | Length of the planning horizon (in years) | 3 years |
| \(\delta_{k,t}\) | Indicator = 1 if a unit invested in product \(k\) at the beginning of year \(t\) finishes **on or before** the end of year 3, otherwise 0. (Used to forbid investments that would not mature in time.) | – |

The numerical values are:

\[
\begin{aligned}
B &= 100\,000,\\
r_1 &= 0.7,\\
r_2 &= 2,\\
L &= 3,\\
\delta_{1,t} &= 1 \quad\forall t\in\{0,1,2\}\;(\text{one‑year product always matures}),\\
\delta_{2,0} &= 1,\;\delta_{2,1}=0,\;\delta_{2,2}=0\;(\text{only a start in year 0 finishes by year 3}).
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 3.  Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{k,t}\) | **Continuous, \(\ge 0\)** | Amount of money (yuan) invested in product \(k\) at the **beginning** of year \(t\). |
| \(y_{k,t}\) | **Binary** | 1 if a *new* investment in product \(k\) is started at year \(t\); 0 otherwise. (Only needed for product 2 to enforce the “multiple‑of‑two‑years” rule.) |

Because the investor can split his capital arbitrarily, the continuous variables alone are sufficient for product 1. For product 2 the binary variable guarantees that the start year respects the “multiple of two” restriction.

---

## 4.  Objective function  

The investor wants to **maximize the total amount of money available at the end of year 3** (initial capital + all realised profits).  

\[
\boxed{\max\; Z \;=\; B \;+\; \sum_{k\in\{1,2\}}\;\sum_{t\in T_k}\; \delta_{k,t}\; r_k \; x_{k,t}}
\]

Explanation  

* For the one‑year product (\(k=1\)), any amount invested in year \(t\) yields a profit of \(r_1 x_{1,t}\) at the end of year \(t+1\). Because the horizon is 3 years, all three start‑years (0, 1, 2) are allowed (\(\delta_{1,t}=1\)).  
* For the two‑year product (\(k=2\)), only an investment started in year 0 matures by the end of year 3, therefore \(\delta_{2,0}=1\) and the other \(\delta_{2,t}=0\).  

The constant term \(B\) simply carries forward the original 100 000 yuan that is not invested (or that is returned together with the profit).

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1  Capital‑availability (cash‑flow) constraints  

The investor cannot spend more cash than he has at the beginning of each year.  
Let \(C_t\) be the cash on hand **at the beginning** of year \(t\).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_0 &= B,\\[2mm]
C_{t+1} &= C_t \;-\; \sum_{k\in\{1,2\}} x_{k,t} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{k\in\{1,2\}} \delta_{k,t-1}\, r_k \, x_{k,t-1}}_{\text{profits that mature at the end of year }t}\qquad\forall t=0,1,2 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The “spending” constraint for each year is simply  

\[
\boxed{ \sum_{k\in\{1,2\}} x_{k,t} \;\le\; C_t \qquad\forall t=0,1,2 } \tag{C1}
\]

Because the cash‑flow equations are linear, they can be expressed directly without introducing the auxiliary \(C_t\) variables, e.g.

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{1,0}+x_{2,0} &\le B, \\[1mm]
x_{1,1}+x_{2,1} &\le B - (x_{1,0}+x_{2,0}) + r_1 x_{1,0}+r_2 x_{2,0}, \\[1mm]
x_{1,2}+x_{2,2} &\le B - (x_{1,0}+x_{2,0}+x_{1,1}+x_{2,1}) + r_1 (x_{1,0}+x_{1,1}) + r_2 x_{2,0}.
\end{aligned}
\]

These three inequalities guarantee that the investor never overdrafts.

### 5.2  “Multiple of two years’’ rule for product 2  

The problem statement requires that the **investment horizon of product 2 be a multiple of two years**. Since the only admissible start‑year that finishes by year 3 is year 0, we enforce:

\[
\boxed{ y_{2,0}=1 \;\Longrightarrow\; x_{2,0}\ge 0 } \qquad
\boxed{ y_{2,0}=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x_{2,0}=0 }
\]

A compact linear formulation uses a big‑\(M\) constant (here \(M=B\) is sufficient because we can never invest more than the total cash):

\[
\begin{aligned}
0 \le x_{2,0} &\le M\, y_{2,0},\\
y_{2,0} &\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{C2}
\]

All other \(y_{2,t}\) for \(t=1,2\) are forced to zero because \(\delta_{2,t}=0\) (they would not mature in time).  

### 5.3  Non‑negativity  

\[
\boxed{x_{k,t}\ge 0\qquad\forall k\in\{1,2\},\;t\in T_k } \tag{C3}
\]

---

## 6.  Full MILP statement  

Putting everything together, the model is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max\; Z \;=&\; B \;+\; r_1\!\sum_{t=0}^{2} x_{1,t} \;+\; r_2\; x_{2,0} \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } 
& x_{1,0}+x_{2,0} \;\le\; B \qquad\text{(year 0 cash)} \\[1mm]
& x_{1,1}+x_{2,1} \;\le\; B - (x_{1,0}+x_{2,0}) + r_1 x_{1,0}+r_2 x_{2,0} \qquad\text{(year 1 cash)}\\[1mm]
& x_{1,2}+x_{2,2} \;\le\; B - (x_{1,0}+x_{2,0}+x_{1,1}+x_{2,1}) + r_1 (x_{1,0}+x_{1,1}) + r_2 x_{2,0} \qquad\text{(year 2 cash)}\\[2mm]
& 0 \le x_{2,0} \le M\, y_{2,0},\qquad y_{2,0}\in\{0,1\} \qquad\text{(two‑year product rule)}\\[2mm]
& x_{k,t}\ge 0 \quad\forall k,t .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7.  Reasonable assumptions made  

| # | Assumption | Reason |
|---|------------|--------|
| A1 | The investor can split his capital arbitrarily (continuous investments). | The statement “invest his 100 000 yuan” does not restrict to integer multiples. |
| A2 | The only feasible start‑year for the two‑year product is **year 0** (because a start in year 1 would finish at the end of year 3, which is allowed, but the “multiple of two years” condition forces the horizon to be exactly 2 years, i.e., start at 0). | This matches the phrasing “investment time must be a multiple of two years”. |
| A3 | No transaction costs, taxes or other fees are considered. | Not mentioned in the problem. |
| A4 | Uninvested cash simply carries forward (no interest). | The problem only gives returns for the two products. |
| A5 | Big‑\(M\) = total capital (100 000) is sufficient to bound the binary‑continuous coupling. | Guarantees the model remains tight. |

---

## 8.  Interpretation of the optimal solution  

Solving the MILP yields the optimal values of \(x_{1,0},x_{1,1},x_{1,2}\) and possibly \(x_{2,0}\).  

*If the solver returns \(x_{2,0}=0\)*, the investor should **invest nothing** in the two‑year product and allocate the whole 100 000 yuan among the one‑year product over the three years (the exact split depends on the cash‑flow constraints).  

*If the solver returns \(x_{2,0}>0\)*, the optimal policy is to put that amount into the two‑year product at the start (year 0) and invest the remaining cash in the one‑year product in the subsequent years.

Because the one‑year product yields a profit of 0.7 yuan per yuan in a single year, while the two‑year product yields 2 yuan per yuan after two years (i.e. an average of 1 yuan per year), the two‑year product is strictly **more profitable** on a per‑year basis. Consequently, the optimal solution will invest the **maximum possible amount** (up to 100 000 yuan) in the two‑year product at year 0, and then invest any leftover cash (if any) in the one‑year product in years 1 and 2.  

Mathematically, the optimal solution is:

\[
\boxed{ x_{2,0}=100\,000,\;\; x_{1,0}=x_{1,1}=x_{1,2}=0 }
\]

which gives a final wealth at the end of year 3 of  

\[
100\,000 + 2 \times 100\,000 = 300\,000\;\text{yuan}.
\]

If, for some reason, the investor is forced to keep a portion of the capital liquid, the model automatically distributes the remaining amount among the one‑year investments while still respecting the cash‑flow constraints.

**Variables**

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 &\ge 0 &&\text{amount (yuan) invested in option 1 at the beginning of year 1}\\
y_1 &\ge 0 &&\text{amount (yuan) invested in option 1 at the beginning of year 2}\\
z_1 &\ge 0 &&\text{amount (yuan) invested in option 1 at the beginning of year 3}\\
x_2 &\ge 0 &&\text{amount (yuan) invested in option 2 at the beginning of year 1}
\end{aligned}
\]

All variables are continuous (the problem is a pure LP).

---

**Cash‑flow expressions (intermediate balances)**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_0 &= 100\,000 \qquad &&\text{initial cash}\\[4pt]
C_1 &= C_0 - x_1 - x_2 + 0.7\,x_1
      = 100\,000 - 0.3\,x_1 - x_2 \qquad &&\text{cash after year 1 (available for year 2)}\\[4pt]
C_2 &= C_1 - y_1 + 0.7\,y_1
      = C_1 - 0.3\,y_1 \qquad &&\text{cash after year 2 (available for year 3)}\\[4pt]
C_3 &= C_2 - z_1 + 0.7\,z_1
      = C_2 - 0.3\,z_1 \qquad &&\text{cash after year 3 before the payoff of option 2}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

**Constraints**

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1) Year‑1 investment limit: } & x_1 + x_2 \le C_0 = 100\,000 \\[4pt]
\text{(2) Year‑2 investment limit: } & y_1 \le C_1 \\[4pt]
\text{(3) Year‑3 investment limit: } & z_1 \le C_2 \\[4pt]
\text{(4) Non‑negativity: } & x_1,\;y_1,\;z_1,\;x_2 \ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

(The constraints (2) and (3) guarantee that the investor never spends more cash than is on hand after the previous year’s returns.)

---

**Objective function – final wealth at the end of year 3**

Option 2 yields a profit of 2 yuan per 1 yuan invested after two full years; the payoff becomes available at the end of year 3. Therefore the final wealth is the cash after year 3 plus the payoff of option 2:

\[
\boxed{\max \; Z = C_3 + 2\,x_2}
\]

Substituting the cash‑flow expressions gives an explicit linear objective:

\[
\begin{aligned}
Z &= \bigl(C_2 - 0.3\,z_1\bigr) + 2\,x_2 \\
  &= \bigl(C_1 - 0.3\,y_1\bigr) - 0.3\,z_1 + 2\,x_2 \\
  &= \bigl(100\,000 - 0.3\,x_1 - x_2\bigr) - 0.3\,y_1 - 0.3\,z_1 + 2\,x_2 \\
  &= 100\,000 - 0.3\,x_1 + 1.7\,x_2 - 0.3\,y_1 - 0.3\,z_1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### Complete Linear Programming Model

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max \;& 100\,000 - 0.3\,x_1 + 1.7\,x_2 - 0.3\,y_1 - 0.3\,z_1 \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\begin{cases}
x_1 + x_2 \le 100\,000 \\
y_1 \le 100\,000 - 0.3\,x_1 - x_2 \\
z_1 \le 100\,000 - 0.3\,x_1 - x_2 - 0.3\,y_1 \\
x_1,\;y_1,\;z_1,\;x_2 \ge 0 .
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

**Assumptions made**

* The profit of option 1 is received at the end of each year and can be reinvested immediately in the next year.
* Option 2 is a two‑year lock‑in; the whole amount (principal + profit) becomes available only at the end of year 3, giving a net return of \(2\,x_2\).
* No transaction costs or other restrictions are considered.

This linear program fully describes the investor’s problem; solving it yields the optimal allocation \((x_1^\*,y_1^\*,z_1^\*,x_2^\*)\) that maximizes the wealth at the end of the third year.

Text:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP) – “Maximum wealth after 3 years”**

The model uses a three‑year horizon ( t = 1,2,3 ).  

| Product | Horizon | Return (profit per unit of capital) | Investment‑timing rule |
|---------|---------|--------------------------------------|------------------------|
| **A**   | 1 year | + 0.7 yuan profit per yuan invested (i.e. 1.7 × principal at year‑end) | Can be started at the beginning of **any** year; the capital (principal + profit) becomes available again at the start of the next year. |
| **B**   | 2 years| + 2 yuan profit per yuan invested (i.e. 3 × principal at the end of the 2‑year period) | Must be started at the beginning of a year and stays locked for exactly two consecutive years. No early withdrawal is allowed. |

The investor starts with **\(C_0 = 100\,000\)** yuan (cash at the beginning of year 1).  
All amounts may be fractional; the decision to start a B‑investment in a given year is binary (either the whole block is started or not).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Meaning | Domain |
|--------|---------|--------|
| \(x_t\) | Amount (yuan) invested in product **A** at the **beginning** of year \(t\) ( \(t=1,2,3\) ) | \(x_t \ge 0\) (continuous) |
| \(y_{12}\) | Amount (yuan) invested in product **B** at the **beginning** of year 1 (covers years 1‑2) | \(y_{12} \ge 0\) (continuous) |
| \(y_{23}\) | Amount (yuan) invested in product **B** at the **beginning** of year 2 (covers years 2‑3) | \(y_{23} \ge 0\) (continuous) |
| \(\delta_{12}\) | Binary indicator: 1 if a B‑investment is started at year 1, 0 otherwise | \(\delta_{12}\in\{0,1\}\) |
| \(\delta_{23}\) | Binary indicator: 1 if a B‑investment is started at year 2, 0 otherwise | \(\delta_{23}\in\{0,1\}\) |

Big‑M linking (any \(M\ge 100\,000\) works, e.g. \(M=100\,000\)):

\[
0\le y_{12}\le M\,\delta_{12},\qquad
0\le y_{23}\le M\,\delta_{23}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Cash‑flow (balance) equations  

Let \(C_t\) be cash **available at the beginning** of year \(t\) (after all receipts from the previous year have been collected).  

*Beginning of year 1*  

\[
C_0 = 100\,000.
\]

*End of year 1 / beginning of year 2*  

- A‑investment made in year 1 returns \(1.7\,x_1\).  
- B‑investment started in year 1 is still locked.  

\[
C_1 = C_0 - y_{12} + 0.7\,x_1.
\]

All cash at the start of year 2 can be re‑allocated:

\[
x_2 + y_{23} \le C_1.
\]

*End of year 2 / beginning of year 3*  

- A‑investment of year 2 returns \(1.7\,x_2\).  
- B‑investment started in year 1 returns \(3\,y_{12}\).  

\[
C_2 = C_1 - y_{23} + 0.7\,x_2 + 3\,y_{12}.
\]

Again, cash at the start of year 3 can be used for A‑investment:

\[
x_3 \le C_2.
\]

*End of year 3 (objective)*  

- A‑investment of year 3 returns \(1.7\,x_3\).  
- B‑investment started in year 2 returns \(3\,y_{23}\).  

Total wealth at the end of year 3:

\[
W = C_2 + 0.7\,x_3 + 3\,y_{23}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. Linear model (compact form)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max \; & W = C_2 + 0.7\,x_3 + 3\,y_{23} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\begin{cases}
C_0 = 100\,000,\\[2pt]
C_1 = C_0 - y_{12} + 0.7\,x_1,\\[2pt]
x_2 + y_{23} \le C_1,\\[2pt]
C_2 = C_1 - y_{23} + 0.7\,x_2 + 3\,y_{12},\\[2pt]
x_3 \le C_2,\\[2pt]
0 \le y_{12} \le M\,\delta_{12},\\[2pt]
0 \le y_{23} \le M\,\delta_{23},\\[2pt]
\delta_{12},\delta_{23}\in\{0,1\},\\[2pt]
x_1,x_2,x_3 \ge 0 .
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

Substituting the definitions of \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) yields an equivalent formulation without auxiliary cash variables:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\max\; & 100\,000 
        + 0.7\,x_1 + 0.7\,x_2 + 0.7\,x_3 
        + 3\,y_{12} + 3\,y_{23}
        - y_{12} - y_{23} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\begin{cases}
x_1 + y_{12} \le 100\,000,\\[2pt]
x_2 + y_{23} \le 100\,000 - y_{12} + 0.7\,x_1,\\[2pt]
x_3 \le 100\,000 - y_{12} - y_{23}
       + 0.7\,x_1 + 0.7\,x_2 + 3\,y_{12},\\[2pt]
0 \le y_{12} \le M\,\delta_{12},\\
0 \le y_{23} \le M\,\delta_{23},\\
\delta_{12},\delta_{23}\in\{0,1\},\\
x_1,x_2,x_3 \ge 0 .
\end{cases}
}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Explanation of components  

*Variables* \(x_t\) – amount placed in the 1‑year product A (continuous).  
*Variables* \(y_{12},y_{23}\) – amount placed in the 2‑year product B (continuous).  
*Binary* \(\delta_{12},\delta_{23}\) – enforce the rule that B‑investments must be taken for a full 2‑year block (big‑M linking).  
*Cash‑flow constraints* – linear equations that exactly track how cash moves from one year to the next, incorporating the returns (0.7 profit per year for A, 2 profit after 2 years for B).  
*Capacity constraints* – ensure you never invest more than the cash you actually have at the start of each year.  
*Objective* – linear expression for total wealth at the end of year 3.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. Solving  

The model is a small MILP (only two binary variables). It can be solved instantly with any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, CBC, GLPK, …).  
The optimal solution provides:

* the optimal amounts \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) to invest in product A each year,  
* whether to start a B‑investment in year 1 (\(\delta_{12}=1\)) and/or year 2 (\(\delta_{23}=1\)), and the corresponding amounts \(y_{12},y_{23}\),  

yielding the maximum possible wealth \(W\) at the end of the third year.

**Linear (MILP) model for the 3‑year investment problem**

---

### 1.  Sets, parameters and decision variables  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(B = 100\,000\) | Initial cash (yuan) at the beginning of year 1. |
| \(r_{1}=0.7\) | Net profit per yuan for **Option 1** (1‑year product).  After one year the invested amount returns \((1+r_{1})=1.7\) yuan. |
| \(r_{2}=2.0\) | Net profit per yuan for **Option 2** (2‑year product).  After two years the invested amount returns \((1+r_{2})=3\) yuan. |
| \(T=\{1,2,3\}\) | Planning horizon – years 1, 2 and 3. |

**Decision variables**

* \(x_{1,t}\ge 0\) – amount (yuan) invested in Option 1 at the **beginning of year \(t\)** \((t=1,2,3)\).  
* \(x_{2,1}\ge 0\) – amount (yuan) invested in Option 2 at the **beginning of year 1** (the only feasible start, because the horizon ends after year 3).  
* \(C_t\ge 0\) – cash on hand at the **beginning of year \(t\)** after all maturities of the previous year have been collected.  
* \(F\ge 0\) – total wealth at the **end of year 3** (objective value).

---

### 2.  Objective  

\[
\boxed{\max \; F}
\]

\(F\) is the amount of money the investor possesses at the end of the third year.

---

### 3.  Constraints  

#### 3.1  Cash‑balance (flow) equations  

*Year 1 (initial cash)*  

\[
C_{1}=B .
\]

*Year 2 – cash after the return of the 1‑year investment made in year 1*  

\[
C_{2}=C_{1}-x_{1,1}-x_{2,1}+(1+r_{1})\,x_{1,1}.
\]

*Year 3 – cash after the return of the 1‑year investment made in year 2 and the 2‑year investment made in year 1*  

\[
C_{3}=C_{2}-x_{1,2}+(1+r_{1})\,x_{1,2}+(1+r_{2})\,x_{2,1}.
\]

#### 3.2  End‑of‑horizon wealth  

All cash that remains at the beginning of year 3 can be kept (no profit can be earned after the horizon).  
Any amount invested in Option 1 at the start of year 3 would not have a full year to mature, therefore it yields **no profit**. Hence

\[
F = C_{3}+x_{1,3}.
\]

(If one prefers to forbid any investment in year 3, simply add the constraint \(x_{1,3}=0\); the model works either way.)

#### 3.3  Investment‑feasibility (cannot invest more than cash available)

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{1,1}+x_{2,1} &\le C_{1},\\
x_{1,2}          &\le C_{2},\\
x_{1,3}          &\le C_{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]

#### 3.4  Non‑negativity  

\[
x_{1,t}\ge 0\;(t=1,2,3),\qquad x_{2,1}\ge 0,\qquad C_{t}\ge 0\;(t=1,2,3),\qquad F\ge 0 .
\]

---

### 4.  Complete linear program  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max \;& F \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
C_{1}=100\,000 \\[2pt]
& C_{2}=C_{1}-x_{1,1}-x_{2,1}+1.7\,x_{1,1} \\[2pt]
& C_{3}=C_{2}-x_{1,2}+1.7\,x_{1,2}+3\,x_{2,1} \\[2pt]
& F = C_{3}+x_{1,3} \\[2pt]
& x_{1,1}+x_{2,1}\le C_{1} \\[2pt]
& x_{1,2}\le C_{2} \\[2pt]
& x_{1,3}\le C_{3} \\[2pt]
& x_{1,1},x_{1,2},x_{1,3},x_{2,1},C_{1},C_{2},C_{3},F \ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All expressions are linear; therefore the formulation is a **linear program**, a special case of an MILP (no integer variables are required).

---

### 5.  How to use the model  

1. Load the model into any LP/MILP solver (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX, CBC, GLPK, or a Python library such as PuLP/​Pyomo).  
2. Solve for the optimal values \((x_{1,1}^{*},x_{1,2}^{*},x_{1,3}^{*},x_{2,1}^{*})\).  
3. The optimal final wealth is \(F^{*}\).  

**Interpretation of the optimal solution**

* \(x_{1,1}^{*}\) – amount to place in the 1‑year, 0.7‑profit product at the start of year 1.  
* \(x_{2,1}^{*}\) – amount to lock for two years (profit = 2 per yuan) at the start of year 1.  
* \(x_{1,2}^{*}\) – amount to reinvest in the 1‑year product at the start of year 2, using the cash that became available after the year‑1 return.  
* \(x_{1,3}^{*}\) – any remaining cash kept at the start of year 3 (no profit earned because the horizon ends).  

The model therefore provides the exact investment schedule that maximizes the investor’s money at the end of the third year.

Text:
**Goal‑programming model for the recruitment problem of Jiali Company**  

The model is a *mixed‑integer linear* goal‑programming (GP) formulation.  
All notation, decision variables, constraints and the goal‑programming objective are given below.  
When a piece of information is not supplied in the statement, a reasonable assumption is explicitly noted.

---

## 1. Sets, indices and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(C=\{1,\dots ,6\}\) | Set of applicant **categories** (Table 4‑4). |
| \(M=\{1,2,3\}\) | Set of **majors** (1 = Major 1, 2 = Major 2, 3 = Major 3). |
| \(L=\{D,N\}\) | Set of **branch locations** ( \(D\)=Donghai, \(N\)=Nanjiang). |
| \(p\in\{1,2,3\}\) | Goal priority level (see the three priorities \(p_{1},p_{2},p_{3}\)). |
| \(a_{c,m}\in\{0,1\}\) | **Competence** – 1 if category \(c\) is competent in major \(m\). |
| \(b_{c,m}\in\{0,1\}\) | **Preferred‑major** – 1 if major \(m\) is the *preferred* major of category \(c\). |
| \(g_{c,l}\in\{0,1\}\) | **Preferred‑city** – 1 if location \(l\) is the *preferred* city of category \(c\). |
| \(d_{l,m}\) | **Demand** of personnel with major \(m\) at location \(l\) (Table 4‑3). |
| \(U_{c}=1500\) | Upper bound on the number of available applicants in each category (Table 4‑4). |
| \(W_{1}=10^{6},\;W_{2}=10^{3},\;W_{3}=10^{3}\) | Goal‑programming weights (large for higher priority).  Any weight satisfying \(W_{1}\gg W_{2}\gg W_{3}\) is admissible. |

The parameter values are obtained directly from the tables:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{c,m}&=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if }m\in\text{Competent Majors of category }c,\\
0 & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}\\[2mm]
b_{c,m}&=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if }m=\text{Preferred Major of category }c,\\
0 & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}\\[2mm]
g_{c,l}&=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if }l=\text{Preferred City of category }c,\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

The demand matrix \(d_{l,m}\) (people) is

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
        & \text{Major 1} & \text{Major 2} & \text{Major 3}\\\hline
\text{Donghai (D)} & 1000 & 2000 & 0\\
\text{Nanjiang (N)}& 2000 & 1000 & 2500\;(1500+1000)\\
\end{array}
\]

(For Donghai, no demand for major 3 is listed, therefore it is taken as 0.)

---

## 2. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Definition | Type |
|--------|------------|------|
| \(x_{c,l,m}\) | Number of recruited persons **from category \(c\)** that are assigned to **location \(l\)** and **major \(m\)**. | Continuous \(\ge 0\) (integrality can be imposed if required). |
| \(d^{+}_{1},d^{-}_{1}\) | Positive/negative deviation from **Goal 1** (total demand satisfaction). | Continuous \(\ge 0\). |
| \(d^{+}_{2},d^{-}_{2}\) | Positive/negative deviation from **Goal 2** (people placed in their preferred major). | Continuous \(\ge 0\). |
| \(d^{+}_{3},d^{-}_{3}\) | Positive/negative deviation from **Goal 3** (people placed in their preferred city). | Continuous \(\ge 0\). |

---

## 3. Model constraints  

### 3.1  Feasibility of competence  
A person can only be assigned to a major for which he/she is competent.

\[
x_{c,l,m}\;\le\; a_{c,m}\;U_{c}\qquad\forall c\in C,\;l\in L,\;m\in M. \tag{C1}
\]

If \(a_{c,m}=0\) the constraint forces \(x_{c,l,m}=0\).

### 3.2  Availability of each category  
The total number taken from a category cannot exceed the pool size.

\[
\sum_{l\in L}\sum_{m\in M} x_{c,l,m}\;\le\;U_{c}\qquad\forall c\in C. \tag{C2}
\]

### 3.3  Demand satisfaction (Goal 1)  
The total number of people assigned to a location–major pair must meet the demand, allowing deviations.

\[
\sum_{c\in C} x_{c,l,m}\;+\;d^{-}_{1,\,l,m}\;-\;d^{+}_{1,\,l,m}\;=\;d_{l,m}\qquad\forall l\in L,\;m\in M. \tag{C3}
\]

For compactness we aggregate the deviations of all location‑major cells into a single pair \((d^{+}_{1},d^{-}_{1})\) by defining  

\[
d^{+}_{1}= \sum_{l,m} d^{+}_{1,\,l,m},\qquad
d^{-}_{1}= \sum_{l,m} d^{-}_{1,\,l,m}.
\]

(If a single overall deviation is preferred, the above can be summed directly.)

### 3.4  Preferred‑major count (Goal 2)  

\[
\sum_{c\in C}\sum_{l\in L}\sum_{m\in M} b_{c,m}\;x_{c,l,m}\;+\;d^{-}_{2}\;-\;d^{+}_{2}\;=\;8000. \tag{C4}
\]

\(d^{-}_{2}\) measures *shortfall* (fewer than 8000 placed in their preferred major),  
\(d^{+}_{2}\) measures *excess* (more than 8000).  In a classic goal‑programming setting only the under‑achievement is penalised; however we keep both deviations to preserve linearity.

### 3.5  Preferred‑city count (Goal 3)  

\[
\sum_{c\in C}\sum_{l\in L}\sum_{m\in M} g_{c,l}\;x_{c,l,m}\;+\;d^{-}_{3}\;-\;d^{+}_{3}\;=\;8000. \tag{C5}
\]

### 3.6  Non‑negativity  

\[
x_{c,l,m}\ge 0,\qquad d^{+}_{p}\ge 0,\;d^{-}_{p}\ge 0\;\;(p=1,2,3). \tag{C6}
\]

---

## 4. Goal‑programming objective  

Goal‑programming minimises a *lexicographic* (priority‑weighted) sum of the undesirable deviations.  
With the weights defined in Section 1:

\[
\boxed{
\min\; Z \;=\; 
W_{1}\,\bigl(d^{+}_{1}+d^{-}_{1}\bigr)\;+\;
W_{2}\,\bigl(d^{+}_{2}+d^{-}_{2}\bigr)\;+\;
W_{3}\,\bigl(d^{+}_{3}+d^{-}_{3}\bigr)
}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

Because \(W_{1}\gg W_{2}\gg W_{3}\) the optimizer first tries to eliminate any deviation from the demand (Goal 1).  Only after the first‑level goal is satisfied (or cannot be improved) does it consider the second‑level goal (preferred majors), and finally the third‑level goal (preferred cities).

If the decision‑maker wishes to **penalise only under‑achievement** for the second and third goals, the objective can be simplified to  

\[
\min\; Z = W_{1}(d^{+}_{1}+d^{-}_{1})+W_{2}d^{-}_{2}+W_{3}d^{-}_{3}.
\]

Both forms are linear and interchangeable.

---

## 5. Summary of the complete MILP model  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\; & Z = 
W_{1}\bigl(d^{+}_{1}+d^{-}_{1}\bigr)
+W_{2}\bigl(d^{+}_{2}+d^{-}_{2}\bigr)
+W_{3}\bigl(d^{+}_{3}+d^{-}_{3}\bigr)\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{c,l,m} b_{c,m}\,x_{c,l,m}+d^{-}_{2}-d^{+}_{2}=8000 \qquad\text{(Goal 2)}\\
&\sum_{c,l,m} g_{c,l}\,x_{c,l,m}+d^{-}_{3}-d^{+}_{3}=8000 \qquad\text{(Goal 3)}\\
&\sum_{c} x_{c,l,m}+d^{-}_{1,\,l,m}-d^{+}_{1,\,l,m}=d_{l,m}\qquad\forall l,m\quad\text{(Goal 1)}\\
&x_{c,l,m}\le a_{c,m}\,U_{c}\qquad\forall c,l,m\\
&\sum_{l,m}x_{c,l,m}\le U_{c}\qquad\forall c\\
&x_{c,l,m},\;d^{+}_{p},d^{-}_{p}\ge 0\qquad\forall c,l,m,\;p=1,2,3.
\end{aligned}
\]

All data needed to instantiate the model are given in the tables; any missing entry (e.g., demand for major 3 in Donghai) has been set to zero, which is a standard assumption when the table does not list a requirement.

The model can be solved with any MILP/LP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, GLPK, …). The optimal solution provides the numbers \(x_{c,l,m}\) – i.e., how many applicants from each category should be hired, in which city and in which major – while respecting the three hierarchical goals of Jiali Company.
